items.answer: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

items.prompt: What is Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED)?
items.answer: Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED) is the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic, head-tracked head-mounted display with a wide field of view.

questions.question: How are the phases in augmented reality's historical evolution described differently from the phases in virtual reality's historical evolution?
options: They can sometimes overlap, unlike the VR phases
They follow a strict single sequence, unlike the VR phases
They are fixed to exact dates, unlike the VR phases
They depend on application domains, unlike the VR phases
questions.explanation: The AR phases are described as broad periods that can sometimes overlap, while the VR phases are not described as doing so. The other options introduce distinctions that are not the stated difference.

questions.question: Which phase of augmented reality's historical evolution focused on enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices?
options: The commercial application phase
The basic research phase
The tools or applications phase
The experimental phase
questions.explanation: The basic research phase centered on enabling AR technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices. The experimental phase defined concepts and required technology types, the tools or applications phase explored early applications and usability, and the commercial application phase involved widespread availability.

data.text: Augmented reality's historical development is divided into four approximate phases that may overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality. These phases show a progression from early work that established concepts and needed technology, through research into tracking, displays, and input devices, then early applications and work on interaction, usability, and design. The timeline ends in commercial application, where AR became more widely available and newer uses appeared in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.
points: Unlike virtual reality's phases, augmented reality's four phases may sometimes overlap: pre-1980s experimental, 1980s–mid-1990s basic research, mid-1990s–2007 tools/applications, 2007–present commercial.
Augmented reality's phases move from concepts, to research into enabling technologies, then applications, usability, and design theory, then commercial availability.

questions.question: How did the first Sutherland-Sproull prototype show computer-generated imagery to the user?
options: By using an external monitor as a virtual environment display
By using a projection screen as an optical see-through display
By using a CRT-based fully immersive virtual display
By using a CRT-based see-through head-mounted display
questions.explanation: The prototype used an optical see-through head-mounted display, so computer-generated imagery could be viewed together with the real world. A fully immersive, external, or projection-based display would not be an optical see-through AR display.

questions.question: What function did the tracking system perform in the first Sutherland-Sproull prototype?
options: It generated virtual environment content in three dimensions
It rendered computer-generated imagery in three dimensions
It registered head movements in three dimensions
It replaced the real-world view in three dimensions
questions.explanation: The tracker registered the user's head movements in three dimensions so the see-through display could reflect those movements. It was not the graphics system that rendered content, generated the virtual environment, or replaced the real-world view.

questions.question: In the super cockpit prototype, how did the pilot's head-mounted display differ between daylight and night or bad weather?
options: It added computer-generated imagery beside the real view in daylight and removed the real view at night or in bad weather
It replaced the real view in daylight and superimposed computer-generated imagery over the real view at night or in bad weather
It superimposed computer-generated imagery over the real view in daylight and replaced the real view at night or in bad weather
It showed only the real view in daylight and showed only computer-generated imagery at night or in bad weather
questions.explanation: In daylight, the computer-generated imagery was superimposed over the real cockpit view, while in night or bad weather it replaced that view. The reversed superimposition/replacement option is the main tempting mistake.

data.text: The experimental phase of augmented reality began with Sutherland and Sproull’s first computer-generated prototype, which combined a see-through head-mounted display with head tracking. The work then moved to the US Air Force super cockpit program, where computer-generated imagery was shown either over the real view or instead of it. These early AR experiments later led to aircraft head-mounted displays, VR displays, and input and tracking hardware.
points: Sutherland and Sproull made the first computer-generated AR prototype in 1968, using a see-through head-mounted display and head tracking.
Tom Furness began research on the US Air Force super cockpit program.
Furness’s super cockpit prototype overlaid computer-generated imagery on daylight views and replaced views at night or bad weather.
Early AR experiments led to modern aircraft head-mounted AR displays, VR displays, and input and tracking hardware.

questions.question: What can be said about the basic research phase of augmented reality relative to earlier work?
options: It followed the mobile applications phase and included much medical visualization work
It preceded the experimentation phase and included much speculative concept work
It preceded the tools development phase and included much outdoor navigation work
It followed the experimentation phase and included much influential 1990s work
questions.explanation: The basic research phase came after the experimentation phase and was marked by influential 1990s research. The other options misplace the phase or attach it to later or unrelated work.

questions.question: What did Chameleon and NaviCam share as early augmented-reality systems?
options: Shared-location display and interaction with the same virtual object
Medical visualization and placement of virtual content inside a patient's body
Handheld mobility and superimposition of virtual content over physical objects
Full virtual immersion and replacement of the physical view with computer-generated scenery
questions.explanation: Chameleon and NaviCam were handheld or mobile systems that showed virtual content over real objects, making them precursors of modern AR applications. The shared-location option describes later shared AR work, not these systems.

questions.question: Which set of contributions was associated with Columbia University during the basic research phase?
options: Registration tracking techniques, see-through display research, and applications alongside basic research
Outdoor GPS interfaces, on-site CAD model creation, and game playing
Virtual cue overlay on stereoscopic video, early AR applications, and shared augmented interaction
An early AR system description, interaction-method work, and mobile AR publications
questions.explanation: Columbia's work included an early paper describing the KARMA system, research on interaction methods, and later publications on mobile AR systems. The other lists belong to different institutions or periods.

data.text: The basic research phase followed early experimentation and was marked by influential 1990s work that shaped augmented reality. Tom Caudell is often credited with coining augmented reality in the first academic article, published in 1992. During this phase, university projects advanced registration tracking, see-through head-mounted displays, interaction methods, applications, and mobile AR, while Chameleon and NaviCam provided early handheld or mobile AR systems and precursors to today’s applications.
points: The basic research phase followed experimentation and shaped augmented reality through influential 1990s work.
Tom Caudell is often credited with coining augmented reality in the first academic article, published in 1992.
University of North Carolina, Columbia, and Toronto research advanced registration tracking, see-through head-mounted displays, interaction, applications, and mobile AR.
Chameleon and NaviCam were early handheld or mobile augmented reality systems and precursors to today’s applications.

questions.question: Why was viewpoint tracking important for augmented reality systems?
options: It let shared content be viewed by people in one place
It let mobile phones show an early augmented application
It let virtual content be registered in three dimensions
It let wearable computers carry information outdoors
questions.explanation: Viewpoint tracking mattered because it let AR content stay registered in three dimensions with the user's view. Sharing content or using it outdoors was a separate application concern, not the purpose of viewpoint tracking.

questions.question: Which capability belonged to medical augmented reality applications from the mid-1990s?
options: Sharing augmented content with people in the same room
Visualizing surgery or X-ray information in a patient's body
Tracking a user's viewpoint with a square marker
Creating CAD models on-site outdoors
questions.explanation: Medical AR work included visualizing laparoscopic surgery, X-rays inside the body, and image-guided surgery. Outdoor CAD, shared nearby content, and marker-based viewpoint tracking are not the medical capabilities described.

questions.question: What mainly made early 2000s wearable augmented reality systems bulky and difficult to use?
options: The amount of data needed to show information in place outdoors
The number of input devices used with the wearable computer setup
The complexity of the software used to track, display, and interact with content
The size of the computer hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and display hardware
questions.explanation: The systems were bulky because of the physical size of their custom hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and displays. Software complexity, data amount, or input-device count are not given as the main cause.

questions.question: What tracking capability did the AR Toolkit provide for augmented reality systems?
options: Real-time viewpoint tracking using a printed cyber code matrix
Real-time GPS-based tracking of a user's position outdoors
Real-time shared tracking of augmented content among nearby users
Real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker
questions.explanation: The AR Toolkit was a tracking library that provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker. It did not provide GPS outdoor tracking, shared multi-user tracking, or cyber-code matrix tracking.

questions.question: What did GPS tracking make possible in early outdoor augmented reality interfaces?
options: Sharing one augmented view with people in the same place
Overlaying AR content on real-world markers for registration
Creating computer-aided design models on-site during a game
Showing information in place in the real world
questions.explanation: GPS tracking let outdoor AR interfaces show information where it belonged in the real world. Marker overlay, shared nearby views, and on-site CAD creation were different AR capabilities.

data.text: During AR’s tools-and-applications phase, mid-1990s work developed core tracking, display, and interaction research while extending AR to shared views, medical uses, and related wearable displays. In 1997, computer-vision markers and GPS wearable computers brought three-dimensional registration to in-place outdoor content. Outdoor wearable AR then supported navigation, CAD, and games in 2002–2003, but its hardware remained bulky and difficult. Marker-tracking advances, including the AR Toolkit, later moved to early mobile phones, where the first mobile-phone AR application appeared in 2004.
points: Mid-1990s AR work included tracking, display, interaction, shared AR content, medical uses, and related wearable head-mounted displays.
In 1997, AR used computer-vision markers and GPS wearable computers to register in-place content in three dimensions.
2002–2003 outdoor wearable AR supported navigation, CAD, and games, but its backpack computers, sensors, and displays were bulky and difficult.
Viewpoint tracking, needed for accurate 3D registration, was addressed by Rekimoto’s matrix tracking and the open-source AR Toolkit’s square-marker tracking.
In 2004, the first mobile-phone AR application was demonstrated, and the AR Toolkit was ported to early mobile phones.

questions.question: Which set of factors moved augmented reality from specialist settings into widely available commercial technology?
options: Smartphone-based AR, improved wearable displays, and AI-based 3D registration
Web-browser AR authoring, smartphone-based AR, and global marketing campaigns
Open-source tracking libraries, marker-based applications, and global marketing campaigns
AR development kits, Android platform support, and holographic projection devices
questions.explanation: The commercial shift was driven by web-browser AR authoring, the arrival of smartphones, and AR use in global marketing campaigns. Later SDKs and future hardware or AI improvements belong to other stages.

questions.question: What effect did the launch of major mobile AR development kits have on commercial AR growth?
options: It let many developers build AR applications, from simple to complex
It let web browsers run AR without smartphone-based tools
It made 3D tracking and registration feasible on low-end devices
It moved AR from specialist applications into widely available commercial technology
questions.explanation: ARKit and ARCore stimulated growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications, expanding the range from simple to complex. They did not themselves make 3D tracking feasible on low-end devices or cause the earlier move from specialist to commercial use.

questions.question: What is expected to make three-dimensional tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices?
options: Development of algorithms, AI, and computer vision technologies
Improvements in wearable, mobile, and holographic projection devices
Launch of AR development kits for major mobile platforms
Use of AR in global marketing campaigns
questions.explanation: Algorithms, artificial intelligence, and computer vision are expected to make 3D tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices. Hardware improvements and earlier commercial drivers contribute to growth but do not make low-end 3D tracking more feasible in the same way.

questions.question: What effect did the launch of an early consumer AR experience have on AR experiences?
options: It helped them start becoming browser-based after earlier low popularity and limited availability
It helped them start becoming popular after earlier low popularity and limited availability
It helped them start becoming smartphone-based after earlier low popularity and limited availability
It helped them start becoming SDK-based after earlier low popularity and limited availability
questions.explanation: The early consumer AR launch helped AR experiences gain popularity after they had been less popular and less available. Browser, smartphone, and SDK-based changes belong to later AR developments.

data.text: The commercial application phase of augmented reality shows a progression from early consumer popularity in 2007 to broader commercial availability in 2009. Web authoring tools, smartphones, and marketing campaigns helped AR move out of research laboratories and specialist use, while Apple and Google development platforms later enabled many developers to build simple and complex AR applications. The phase remains ongoing, and further growth is expected as devices, tools, artificial intelligence, and computer vision improve.
points: The commercial application phase of augmented reality began in 2007, when AR experiences started becoming much more popular.
In 2009, augmented reality moved from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology.
Main factors behind augmented reality's 2009 commercial move were web-based AR authoring tools, smartphones, and global marketing campaigns.
From 2017, Apple’s ARKit and Google’s Android ARCore enabled many developers to create simple and complex AR applications.
The commercial application phase of augmented reality continues, expected to grow with more tools, devices, AI, and computer vision.

questions.question: For which topic is the 2015 article by Billinghurst et al. recommended as a more detailed source?
options: The upcoming issues and challenges in XR
The hardware and software used in virtual reality
The optimization of XR resource requirements
The historical evolution of augmented reality
questions.explanation: The article is recommended specifically for a more detailed account of augmented reality's historical evolution. It is not the recommended source for the upcoming issues-and-challenges topic, VR hardware and software, or XR resource optimization.

data.text: The historical evolution of augmented reality can be followed in greater depth using the 2015 article by Billinghurst et al. This recommended source supplies a more detailed account of how augmented reality developed. It then leads toward the next lecture on issues and challenges.
points: The 2015 Billinghurst et al. article is a recommended source for a more detailed account of augmented reality's historical evolution.

questions.question: How does the basic research phase of augmented reality extend the experimental phase?
questions.reference_answer: The basic research phase extends the experimental phase by moving from identifying what augmented reality requires to researching the enabling technologies that make it possible. The experimental phase defined augmented reality concepts and showed the types of technology required for augmented reality. The basic research phase then involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.

questions.question: What makes Chameleon and NaviCam precursors to the kind of augmented-reality applications seen today?
questions.reference_answer: They were early handheld or mobile augmented-reality systems that superimposed virtual content on the real world. Chameleon allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display over paper to see virtual content, and NaviCam superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld or head-mounted displays. Because both were true augmented-reality-type applications, they anticipated the kind of augmented-reality applications seen today.

questions.question: How did augmented reality become widely available commercial technology after The Eye of Judgment was released?
questions.reference_answer: It became widely available because a consumer launch made augmented reality popular and later commercial factors removed its earlier barriers. The Eye of Judgment, released in 2007, began the commercial application phase and made such augmented-reality experiences popular after augmented reality had previously been neither very popular nor easily available. In 2009, Adobe Flash authoring tools, smartphone-based augmented reality, and global marketing campaigns moved augmented reality from research laboratories and specialist applications to widespread commercial use.
